ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Ethical approval was granted by the University of Hull Faculty of Health Sciences Ethics Committee (Ref. 2018-PSY-14).
table.formatted: Ethical approval was granted by the University of Hull Faculty of Health Sciences Ethics Committee <ref type="bibr">(Ref. 2018-PSY-14)</ref>.

table.text: Participants were assigned to either an AM-PM schedule (Session 1 in the morning and Session 2 in the evening) or a PM-AM schedule (Session 1 in the evening and Session 2 the following morning).
Participants were recruited from the undergraduate Psychology degree programme at the University of Hull.
Participants provided electronic informed consent and received course credit.
Participants completed a demographics questionnaire assessing birth year, gender, handedness, native language (language spoken mostly at home while growing up), vision status, and hearing status.
Participants were instructed to memorise each pair by imagining a vivid interaction between the objects (e.g., "imagine the match-stick setting fire to the tube of glue").
During encoding and the immediate test, participants were not told that indirect A-C associations would later be tested.
Participants had up to 5,000 ms to choose the object they believed had been paired with the cue.
Participants were offered brief breaks during the test, including optional 20 s break screens.
All participants were asked to refrain from daytime sleep during the interval and to avoid excessive caffeine or alcohol.
Before the delayed test, participants were told for the first time that both direct and indirect association trials would appear.
Trials were pseudorandomised to intermix direct and indirect items, and participants were offered brief breaks during the test, including optional 20 s break screens.

Participants were flagged and excluded if any of the following held, with z scores computed across complete cases before behavioural exclusions and using participant-level summaries of direct trials only: (a) direct accuracy at T1 was an extreme low outlier (z < -2.5); (b) direct accuracy at T2 was an extreme low outlier (z < -2.5) with acceptable T1 accuracy (z at T1 ≥ -2.0); (c) the proportion of timeouts at T1 or T2 was an extreme high outlier (z > 2.5), where a timeout was defined as no response within 5,000 ms; or (d) mean T1 choice RT was an extreme low outlier (z < -2.5).
table.formatted: Participants were flagged and excluded if any of the following held, with z scores computed across complete cases before behavioural exclusions and using participant-level summaries of direct trials only: (a) direct accuracy at T1 was an extreme low outlier (z < -2.5); (b) direct accuracy at T2 was an extreme low outlier (z < -2.5) with acceptable T1 accuracy (z at T1 ≥ -2.0); (c) the proportion of timeouts at T1 or T2 was an extreme high outlier (z > 2.5), where a timeout was defined as no response within 5,000 ms; or (d) mean T1 choice RT was an extreme low outlier (z < -2.5).

table.text: Of the 209 complete cases, 24 participants were flagged and excluded at the initial protocol and behavioural QC stage.
Descriptively, SSS ratings were similar at Session 1 (AM-PM M = 3.07, SD = 1.25; PM-AM M = 3.37, SD = 1.21; one AM-PM participant had no Session 1 rating).

Because participants were told at T2 that indirect trials would appear, these ratings are best interpreted as subjective judgements about how they made each choice, rather than as direct evidence that an A-C relation had been stored as a new memory.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Participants were assigned to either an AM-PM schedule (Session 1 in the morning and Session 2 in the evening) or a PM-AM schedule (Session 1 in the evening and Session 2 the following morning).

> Participants were recruited from the undergraduate Psychology degree programme at the University of Hull.

> Participants provided electronic informed consent and received course credit.

> Participants completed a demographics questionnaire assessing birth year, gender, handedness, native language (language spoken mostly at home while growing up), vision status, and hearing status.

> Participants were instructed to memorise each pair by imagining a vivid interaction between the objects (e.g., "imagine the match-stick setting fire to the tube of glue").

> During encoding and the immediate test, participants were not told that indirect A-C associations would later be tested.

> Participants had up to 5,000 ms to choose the object they believed had been paired with the cue.

> Participants were offered brief breaks during the test, including optional 20 s break screens.

> All participants were asked to refrain from daytime sleep during the interval and to avoid excessive caffeine or alcohol.

> Before the delayed test, participants were told for the first time that both direct and indirect association trials would appear.

> Trials were pseudorandomised to intermix direct and indirect items, and participants were offered brief breaks during the test, including optional 20 s break screens.

> Participants were flagged and excluded if any of the following held, with z scores computed across complete cases before behavioural exclusions and using participant-level summaries of direct trials only: (a) direct accuracy at T1 was an extreme low outlier (z < -2.5); (b) direct accuracy at T2 was an extreme low outlier (z < -2.5) with acceptable T1 accuracy (z at T1 ≥ -2.0); (c) the proportion of timeouts at T1 or T2 was an extreme high outlier (z > 2.5), where a timeout was defined as no response within 5,000 ms; or (d) mean T1 choice RT was an extreme low outlier (z < -2.5).

> Of the 209 complete cases, 24 participants were flagged and excluded at the initial protocol and behavioural QC stage.

> Descriptively, SSS ratings were similar at Session 1 (AM-PM M = 3.07, SD = 1.25; PM-AM M = 3.37, SD = 1.21; one AM-PM participant had no Session 1 rating).

> Because participants were told at T2 that indirect trials would appear, these ratings are best interpreted as subjective judgements about how they made each choice, rather than as direct evidence that an A-C relation had been stored as a new memory.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

codebook_check.title: Codebook Check
codebook_check.summary_text:
-  We parsed 21 variable definitions from codebook/README files.
-  4 of 129 data columns (3%) are documented in a codebook; 125 are not.
-  A codebook was found and parsed (21 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 3% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents `\`id\``, `\`group\``, `\`session\`` while the data has `id`, `group`, `session`. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.

report: This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.
We examined 3 codebook/README/label sources and 129 data columns across 18 files.

**A codebook was found and parsed (21 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 3% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents `\`id\``, `\`group\``, `\`session\`` while the data has `id`, `group`, `session`. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.**

ownership.dep_title: No Evidence That Overnight Sleep Improves Associative Inference
ownership.dep_description: Data, analysis code and fitted models for Wibroe and Lindsay, "No Evidence That Overnight Sleep Improves Associative Inference". The study tested whether a 12-hour interval containing overnight sleep improves direct associative memory and A-C inference relative to a daytime interval of the same length. Participants completed an online paired-associate inference task with overlapping A-B and B-C object pairs. Direct pairs were tested immediately and after the delay; novel A-C inference trials were tested after the delay. The package contains de-identified trial-level and participant-level data with a codebook, the analysis scripts, the fitted Bayesian models, and the figures, tables and summary values reported in the paper.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 129 columns across 18 data files.
#### Issues Identified
9 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("banino_monotonic_preds.rds", "banino_monotonic_preds.rds", "banino_monotonic_preds.rds", "h4_source_cumulative_preds.rds", "h4_source_cumulative_preds.rds", "h4_source_cumulative_preds.rds", "h7_rt_choice_gaussian_preds.rds", "h7_rt_choice_gaussian_preds.rds", "h7_rt_choice_gaussian_preds.rds"), Column = c("mean", "q025", "q975", "mean", "q025", "q975", "mean", "q025", "q975"), Issues = c("⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 1 value is missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 1 value is missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 1 value is missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 1 value is missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 1 value is missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 1 value is missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 1 value is missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 1 value is missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 1 value is missing" )), row.names = c(NA, -9L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 18 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

summary_table.ethics_statements: Ethical approval was granted by the University of Hull Faculty of Health Sciences Ethics Committee (Ref. 2018-PSY-14).
live_data_statements: Participants were assigned to either an AM-PM schedule (Session 1 in the morning and Session 2 in the evening) or a PM-AM schedule (Session 1 in the evening and Session 2 the following morning).
Participants were recruited from the undergraduate Psychology degree programme at the University of Hull.
Participants provided electronic informed consent and received course credit.
Participants completed a demographics questionnaire assessing birth year, gender, handedness, native language (language spoken mostly at home while growing up), vision status, and hearing status.
Participants were instructed to memorise each pair by imagining a vivid interaction between the objects (e.g., "imagine the match-stick setting fire to the tube of glue").
During encoding and the immediate test, participants were not told that indirect A-C associations would later be tested.
Participants had up to 5,000 ms to choose the object they believed had been paired with the cue.
Participants were offered brief breaks during the test, including optional 20 s break screens.
All participants were asked to refrain from daytime sleep during the interval and to avoid excessive caffeine or alcohol.
Before the delayed test, participants were told for the first time that both direct and indirect association trials would appear.
Trials were pseudorandomised to intermix direct and indirect items, and participants were offered brief breaks during the test, including optional 20 s break screens.

Participants were flagged and excluded if any of the following held, with z scores computed across complete cases before behavioural exclusions and using participant-level summaries of direct trials only: (a) direct accuracy at T1 was an extreme low outlier (z < -2.5); (b) direct accuracy at T2 was an extreme low outlier (z < -2.5) with acceptable T1 accuracy (z at T1 ≥ -2.0); (c) the proportion of timeouts at T1 or T2 was an extreme high outlier (z > 2.5), where a timeout was defined as no response within 5,000 ms; or (d) mean T1 choice RT was an extreme low outlier (z < -2.5).
Of the 209 complete cases, 24 participants were flagged and excluded at the initial protocol and behavioural QC stage.
Descriptively, SSS ratings were similar at Session 1 (AM-PM M = 3.07, SD = 1.25; PM-AM M = 3.37, SD = 1.21; one AM-PM participant had no Session 1 rating).

Because participants were told at T2 that indirect trials would appear, these ratings are best interpreted as subjective judgements about how they made each choice, rather than as direct evidence that an A-C relation had been stored as a new memory.

> mo_draw_score <- function(draws, simplex_prefix, step) {
>   simplex_cols <- grep(
>     paste0("^", gsub("([\\[\\]\\(\\)\\{\\}\\+\\*\\?\\^\\$\\.\\|])", "\\\\\\1", simplex_prefix), "\\["),
>     names(draws),
>     value = TRUE
>   )
>   n_steps <- length(simplex_cols)
>   if (n_steps < 1L) {
>     stop("Missing monotonic simplex draws for: ", simplex_prefix)
>   }
>   if (step < 0L || step > n_steps) {
>     stop("Monotonic step ", step, " is outside 0:", n_steps, " for ", simplex_prefix)
>   }
>   if (step == 0L) {
>     return(rep(0, nrow(draws)))
>   }
>   step_cols <- paste0(simplex_prefix, "[", seq_len(step), "]")
>   n_steps * rowSums(as.matrix(draws[, step_cols, drop = FALSE]))
> }

info.title: No evidence that overnight sleep improves associative inference

author.affiliation:

text.text: Sleep can help preserve learned associations, but evidence that it also helps people draw new inferences from them is mixed.
We tested both outcomes in the same task, comparing performance after a 12-hour overnight interval with performance after a daytime interval of the same length.
In an online experiment, participants learned overlapping object pairs (A-B and B-C) and were tested on them immediately and again after the delay.
Only at the delayed test were they asked to infer the relationship between objects linked through the shared item (A-C).
We analysed accuracy and response times using Bayesian multilevel models.
Memory for the learned pairs declined in both groups, and inference accuracy remained close to chance.
Inferences were more likely to be correct when participants also recognised both of the pairs needed to make them.
Overall, the results gave no clear evidence of an overnight benefit for memory or inference and were consistent with participants retrieving and combining the learned pairs at test.
Episodic memory supports more than memory for individual episodes.
It also allows people to derive new relations from overlapping experiences.

A standard test of this flexibility is A-C inference, in which people learn overlapping A-B and B-C pairs and later identify the related C item for A, despite never having encountered them together (Banino et al., 2016; Zeithamova & Preston, 2010).
text.formatted: A standard test of this flexibility is A-C inference, in which people learn overlapping A-B and B-C pairs and later identify the related C item for A, despite never having encountered them together <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Banino et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Zeithamova & Preston, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Successful A-C inference could arise through several, potentially co-occurring routes, including an integrated representation formed during encoding (Schlichting & Preston, 2015; Shohamy & Wagner, 2008), an integrated representation strengthened or reorganised through offline consolidation (Lewis & Durrant, 2011; Tadros & Bazhenov, 2022), or retrieval and recombination of the premise memories at test (Banino et al., 2016; Zeithamova & Preston, 2010).
text.formatted: Successful A-C inference could arise through several, potentially co-occurring routes, including an integrated representation formed during encoding <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Schlichting & Preston, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Shohamy & Wagner, 2008)</ref>, an integrated representation strengthened or reorganised through offline consolidation <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Lewis & Durrant, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Tadros & Bazhenov, 2022)</ref>, or retrieval and recombination of the premise memories at test <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Banino et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Zeithamova & Preston, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The retrieval-based recombination account posits that inference is constructed at test rather than stored as a direct A-C association (Banino et al., 2016; Zeithamova & Preston, 2010).
text.formatted: The retrieval-based recombination account posits that inference is constructed at test rather than stored as a direct A-C association <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Banino et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Zeithamova & Preston, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: When faced with a novel query such as the relationship between A and C, the learner retrieves the separate A-B and B-C associations and combines them in working memory.
This process relies on the constructive nature of episodic memory.
The hippocampus reinstates distinct memory fragments and binds them in service of current goals (Preston & Eichenbaum, 2013).
text.formatted: The hippocampus reinstates distinct memory fragments and binds them in service of current goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Preston & Eichenbaum, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Neuroimaging evidence is consistent with this view, linking successful novel inference to activation in a hippocampal-ventromedial prefrontal circuit during retrieval-mediated learning (Zeithamova et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Neuroimaging evidence is consistent with this view, linking successful novel inference to activation in a hippocampal-ventromedial prefrontal circuit during retrieval-mediated learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Zeithamova et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: This account predicts that A-C inference should be slower and less accurate than direct associative recognition because it requires coordinated retrieval of both premises via the shared B item.
It also predicts that inference should be vulnerable when either premise is inaccessible or weak (Banino et al., 2016; Zeithamova & Preston, 2010).
text.formatted: It also predicts that inference should be vulnerable when either premise is inaccessible or weak <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Banino et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Zeithamova & Preston, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: A prominent alternative is that offline consolidation, particularly sleep, can promote integration across overlapping episodes.

Active systems consolidation theories propose that hippocampal reactivation during slow-wave sleep supports the redistribution and reorganisation of recently encoded memories (Diekelmann & Born, 2010; Klinzing et al., 2019; Rasch & Born, 2013).
text.formatted: Active systems consolidation theories propose that hippocampal reactivation during slow-wave sleep supports the redistribution and reorganisation of recently encoded memories <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Diekelmann & Born, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Klinzing et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Rasch & Born, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: For overlapping pairs, repeated coactivation of A-B and B-C traces could, in principle, strengthen their shared structure.

This might support an A-C representation that depends less on explicit retrieval of both premises, either as a direct associative shortcut or as a more generalised triad representation (Lewis & Durrant, 2011; Stickgold & Walker, 2013).
text.formatted: This might support an A-C representation that depends less on explicit retrieval of both premises, either as a direct associative shortcut or as a more generalised triad representation <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Lewis & Durrant, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Stickgold & Walker, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Computational models of paired-associate learning similarly suggest that replay of overlapping traces can increase generalisation to novel A-C queries without additional experience at encoding (Tadros & Bazhenov, 2022).
text.formatted: Computational models of paired-associate learning similarly suggest that replay of overlapping traces can increase generalisation to novel A-C queries without additional experience at encoding <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Tadros & Bazhenov, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Studies that experimentally manipulate reactivation provide an important source of evidence that offline reactivation can support later memory and inference.
For example, targeted memory reactivation during slow-wave sleep can strengthen cued memories (Hu et al., 2020).
text.formatted: For example, targeted memory reactivation during slow-wave sleep can strengthen cued memories <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Hu et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In relational paradigms, targeted reactivation can enhance subsequent relational learning and inference (Santamaria et al., 2024), and targeted reactivation of A-B and B-C pairs during offline rest can selectively enhance subsequent A-C inference (Shearer et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In relational paradigms, targeted reactivation can enhance subsequent relational learning and inference <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Santamaria et al., 2024)</ref>, and targeted reactivation of A-B and B-C pairs during offline rest can selectively enhance subsequent A-C inference <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Shearer et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These findings show that externally cued reactivation can support integration across overlapping memories.
Whether comparable integration occurs during typical, uncued sleep remains unclear.

If uncued overnight sleep promotes integration, post-sleep performance should show signatures beyond accuracy, including a reduced response time cost for A-C decisions and weaker dependence on the accessibility of the premise associations linked by the shared B item.

Early behavioural work suggested that sleep can benefit relational generalisation. Ellenbogen et al. (2007) reported that while immediate inference was poor, a delay containing nocturnal sleep improved performance on hierarchical inferences relative to a matched wake interval.
text.formatted: Early behavioural work suggested that sleep can benefit relational generalisation. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Ellenbogen et al. (2007)</ref> reported that while immediate inference was poor, a delay containing nocturnal sleep improved performance on hierarchical inferences relative to a matched wake interval.

text.text: Related studies reported nap-associated gains in A-C inference (Alger & Payne, 2016; Lau et al., 2011) and transitive inference after sleep (Werchan & Gómez, 2013).
text.formatted: Related studies reported nap-associated gains in A-C inference <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Alger & Payne, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Lau et al., 2011)</ref> and transitive inference after sleep <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Werchan & Gómez, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: These findings motivated the view that sleep may help extract shared structure from overlapping experiences, although later work has highlighted important boundary conditions.
More recent work suggests that any benefits after sleep may depend on encoding strength and task structure.
Evidence across tasks that assess associative inference and related forms of generalisation is mixed, with effects varying across learning conditions and outcome measures (Lerner & Gluck, 2019).
text.formatted: Evidence across tasks that assess associative inference and related forms of generalisation is mixed, with effects varying across learning conditions and outcome measures <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Lerner & Gluck, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: For example, a conference report found no effect of a nap on transitive inference (Morgan & Stickgold, 2017).
text.formatted: For example, a conference report found no effect of a nap on transitive inference <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Morgan & Stickgold, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Sleep effects may also depend on inference complexity, sometimes described as relational distance. Foldes et al. (2023) reported that improvements after sleep in transitive inference were most robust when relationships spanned multiple intermediate links and when initial learning was strong but not saturated.
text.formatted: Sleep effects may also depend on inference complexity, sometimes described as relational distance. <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Foldes et al. (2023)</ref> reported that improvements after sleep in transitive inference were most robust when relationships spanned multiple intermediate links and when initial learning was strong but not saturated.

text.text: Conversely, in a visual paired-associate task, Schmidig et al. (2024) found benefits after sleep for recognition discrimination but no reliable benefit for associative cued recall.
text.formatted: Conversely, in a visual paired-associate task, <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Schmidig et al. (2024)</ref> found benefits after sleep for recognition discrimination but no reliable benefit for associative cued recall.

text.text: In a separate episodic-abstraction task, Talamini et al. (2022) found benefits after sleep for arbitrary associations but no preferential benefit for associative regularities or generalisation.
text.formatted: In a separate episodic-abstraction task, <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Talamini et al. (2022)</ref> found benefits after sleep for arbitrary associations but no preferential benefit for associative regularities or generalisation.

text.text: This mixed pattern suggests that if sleep supports integration across overlapping memories, the effect is likely to depend on task conditions.

Apparent gains after sleep in inference could reflect the formation of new integrated structures, but they could also arise indirectly if sleep better preserves the A-B and B-C premises needed for recombination.
Distinguishing these possibilities requires going beyond accuracy to examine the decision processes underlying A-C responses.
Response times, source ratings, and premise dependence can provide converging evidence about whether A-C decisions rely mainly on retrieval-based recombination or on a more integrated representation.

Under a recombination account, A-C choices should show a response time cost relative to direct pairs and should be constrained by access to the two premise associations via the shared B item (Banino et al., 2016; Zeithamova & Preston, 2010).
text.formatted: Under a recombination account, A-C choices should show a response time cost relative to direct pairs and should be constrained by access to the two premise associations via the shared B item <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Banino et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Zeithamova & Preston, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: A-C choices should be more accurate when both premises are accessible, with the less accessible premise acting as a potential bottleneck.

By contrast, if offline consolidation promotes an A-C representation that reduces the need for explicit chaining, the response time cost of A-C decisions should diminish and premise dependence should be attenuated.

Source ratings provided a complementary source-monitoring measure by indexing whether A-C choices were experienced as indirect inferences from the studied pairs or as associations with a more direct subjective basis (Johnson et al., 1993).
text.formatted: Source ratings provided a complementary source-monitoring measure by indexing whether A-C choices were experienced as indirect inferences from the studied pairs or as associations with a more direct subjective basis <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Johnson et al., 1993)</ref>.

text.text: Given mixed prior evidence, we treated predictions based on source ratings as exploratory and interpreted them alongside response times and measures of premise dependence.
We tested these ideas using a web-based paired-associate inference task.

Participants learned overlapping object pairs (A-B and B-C) and were tested after an approximately 12-hour AM-PM or PM-AM schedule, providing a daytime-wake versus overnight sleep-opportunity contrast.
text.formatted: Participants learned overlapping object pairs <ref type="bibr">(A-B and B-C)</ref> and were tested after an approximately 12-hour AM-PM or PM-AM schedule, providing a daytime-wake versus overnight sleep-opportunity contrast.

text.text: To reduce immediate test-induced learning, we presented the inferential A-C test only in the second session.
This design assessed delayed A-C inference without prior A-C test exposure, although it did not provide a baseline measure of immediate A-C performance.

We therefore asked whether the PM-AM schedule benefited retention of directly learned premise pairs (H1), improved delayed A-C inference (H2-H3), or altered the processes supporting inference, including retrieval fluency, source attribution, and premise dependence (H4-H6).
Our hypotheses are presented below.

If sleep stabilises recently encoded episodic traces, then the decline in accuracy for direct pairs (A-B and B-C) from the immediate test (T1) to the delayed test (T2) should be smaller after an interval containing sleep than after wakefulness.
We tested this as a Group (PM-AM vs.
AM-PM) × Time (Immediate vs.
Delayed) interaction.
If participants can derive the novel A-C relation after the delay, A-C accuracy should exceed chance.
If the overnight PM-AM schedule facilitates integration of overlapping episodes into a unified representation, delayed A-C accuracy should be higher in the PM-AM group than in the AM-PM group.

If sleep makes A-C inference less dependent on stepwise retrieval of the studied pairs, the response time cost for A-C choices relative to direct-pair choices should be smaller in the PM-AM group than in the AM-PM group.
We tested this as the schedule difference in the A-C versus direct-pair RT contrast.
The PM-AM schedule may alter how A-C choices are subjectively attributed.
If sleep promotes integration or unitisation of overlapping memories, A-C pairs may feel directly known and be misattributed to direct study.

Conversely, if sleep strengthens episodic detail for the premise pairs, participants may better recognise that A and C were never encountered together and attribute A-C decisions to an indirect source.

Because both outcomes are theoretically plausible, we treated source attribution for A-C trials as exploratory and tested whether subjective source ratings differed between the PM-AM and AM-PM groups.
Under a retrieval-based recombination account, A-C success should depend partly on access to the premise associations and on how successfully recognised premises are subjectively attributed.

We expected higher direct-source ratings for recognised premise pairs to be associated with higher A-C accuracy, but tested whether this association was weaker in the PM-AM group (Group × Source Attribution interaction), as predicted if integration reduces reliance on premise retrieval on each trial.
Retrieval-based recombination is strongly constrained by the availability of the premise memories.
We tested whether A-C success was strongly constrained by the quantity (number of correct premises) and quality (strength of the weakest premise) of the direct associations.

While we expected positive associations in both cases, we tested whether sleep reduced dependence on premise availability, predicting that the dependence of inference on specific premise availability would be reduced in the PM-AM group.
The study used a two-session web-based paired-associate inference task with a 12hour interval between sessions.
Participants were assigned to either an AM-PM schedule (Session 1 in the morning and Session 2 in the evening) or a PM-AM schedule (Session 1 in the evening and Session 2 the following morning).
Premise memory for trained pairs (A-B and B-C) was assessed at both the immediate test (T1) and the delayed test (T2).
A-C inference was assessed at T2 only using novel A-C trials derived from the overlapping A-B and B-C pairs.
Primary outcomes were two-alternative forced choice (2AFC) accuracy and choice RT.
Secondary measures included T1 confidence ratings and T2 source ratings indicating whether each association felt directly learned or indirectly inferred.
We aimed to recruit at least N = 200 participants, with approximately n = 100 per schedule group, a target based on recruitment feasibility.
A total of N = 216 participants began the study, of whom N = 209 completed both sessions.
After the exclusions described below, the main analysis sample comprised N = 167, with AM-PM n = 75 and PM-AM n = 92 (age M = 19.6 years, SD = 4.8; 126 women, 38 men, and 3 reporting another gender).
Participants were recruited from the undergraduate Psychology degree programme at the University of Hull.
Inclusion criteria were normal or corrected-to-normal vision, fluency in English, no self-reported neurological or psychiatric disorder, and no diagnosed sleep disorder.
Participants provided electronic informed consent and received course credit.
Ethical approval was granted by the University of Hull Faculty of Health Sciences Ethics Committee (Ref. 2018-PSY-14).
text.formatted: Ethical approval was granted by the University of Hull Faculty of Health Sciences Ethics Committee <ref type="bibr">(Ref. 2018-PSY-14)</ref>.

text.text: Stimuli were 60 black-and-white line drawings of common objects drawn from the black-and-white line-drawing subset of the Bank of Standardized Stimuli (Brodeur et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Stimuli were 60 black-and-white line drawings of common objects drawn from the black-and-white line-drawing subset of the Bank of Standardized Stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Brodeur et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Objects were arranged into 20 triplets (A-B-C) by manual inspection to minimise obvious semantic or visual similarity within pairs and across triplets.
This yielded 40 direct pairs (20 A-B, 20 B-C) for encoding, with each B object appearing in both pairings to enable testing of 20 novel A-C inferences.
The experiment was implemented using the Gorilla online experimental platform (Anwyl-Irvine et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The experiment was implemented using the Gorilla online experimental platform <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Anwyl-Irvine et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Participation was restricted to desktop browsers.
Sessions ran full-screen at participants' native resolution, and responses were collected via mouse clicks.
Participants completed a demographics questionnaire assessing birth year, gender, handedness, native language (language spoken mostly at home while growing up), vision status, and hearing status.

A delay-interval questionnaire measured sleep occurrence during the 12-hour delay (yes/no, including naps), sleep duration (categorical scale from < 1 hour to 11-12 hours), bedtime and sleep onset times, number of awakenings (none to 6+ times), final wake time, sleep quality rating (6-point scale from "very badly" to "very well"), sleep problems (open text entry), and substance use during the delay period.
text.formatted: A delay-interval questionnaire measured sleep occurrence during the 12-hour delay (yes/no, including naps), sleep duration (categorical scale from < 1 hour to 11-12 hours), bedtime and sleep onset times, number of awakenings (none to 6+ times), final wake time, sleep quality rating (6-point scale from "very badly" to "very well"), sleep problems (open text entry), and substance use during the delay period.

text.text: Current sleepiness was assessed using the Stanford Sleepiness Scale [SSS; Hoddes et al. (1973)], a 7-point scale ranging from 1 ("Feeling active/vital/alert or wide awake") to 7 ("No longer fighting sleep; sleep onset soon; having dream-like thoughts").
text.formatted: Current sleepiness was assessed using the Stanford Sleepiness Scale [SSS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Hoddes et al. (1973)</ref>], a 7-point scale ranging from 1 ("Feeling active/vital/alert or wide awake") to 7 ("No longer fighting sleep; sleep onset soon; having dream-like thoughts").

text.text: A schematic of the schedule and task structure is shown in Figure 1.
text.formatted: A schematic of the schedule and task structure is shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>.

text.text: Note.
Participants encoded overlapping A-B and B-C object pairs and completed an immediate test of the trained pairs in Session 1 (T1), with confidence ratings after each response.

Participants then completed either an AM-PM daytime interval or a PM-AM overnight interval before Session 2 (T2), which included delayed tests of direct A-B and B-C associations and novel A-C inference trials.
T2 source ratings assessed whether participants judged each selected association as directly experienced or indirectly inferred.
Participants first viewed on-screen instructions, followed by a short practice block using non-experimental objects.
Participants were instructed to memorise each pair by imagining a vivid interaction between the objects (e.g., "imagine the match-stick setting fire to the tube of glue").
The instructions included an example trial.
Participants then completed the demographics questionnaire before beginning the encoding phase.
The encoding phase comprised 80 trials in total using spaced repetition with A-B and B-C pairs presented in alternating blocks.
Block 1 presented all 20 A-B pairs (first exposure), followed by Block 2 with all 20 B-C pairs (first exposure).
After a 60 s halfway break, Block 3 presented all 20 A-B pairs and Block 4 presented all 20 B-C pairs again.
Within each block, trial order was randomised.
On every encoding trial, the two objects were presented side by side for 6 s, preceded by a 500-ms fixation cross.
The left-right positions of the two objects were counterbalanced across encoding trials.
An 8 s break occurred after every 10 trials.
No overt response was required during encoding, and participants received no feedback.
During encoding and the immediate test, participants were not told that indirect A-C associations would later be tested.
The first session then included a 40-trial recognition test on the trained pairs (20 A-B and 20 B-C).

Each trial began with a 500-ms fixation cross, followed by a cue object on the left and two choice objects on the right, one being the studied associate and the other a previously studied foil from another triplet.
A objects cued A-B trials, and B objects cued B-C trials.
Participants had up to 5,000 ms to choose the object they believed had been paired with the cue.
They then rated their confidence on a 3-point scale (1 = "Definitely correct",2 = "Probably correct",3 = "Just guessing"), so lower values indicated higher confidence.
Target position was balanced across trials, and foils were selected to minimise obvious within-triplet overlap.
Participants were offered brief breaks during the test, including optional 20 s break screens.
No corrective feedback was given.
Participants then provided an email address to receive the Session 2 link.
Participants in the AM-PM group completed Session 1 in the morning and returned approximately 12 h later in the evening.
Those in the PM-AM group completed Session 1 in the evening and returned approximately 12 h later the following morning.
Because sessions were completed remotely, actual start times varied around the intended morning and evening schedule.

The analysis therefore defined protocol adherence using the elapsed intersession delay, calculated from the first recorded choice-trial timestamp in Session 1 to the first recorded choice-trial timestamp in Session 2.
Participants with an intersession delay of 18 h or longer were classified as out of protocol and excluded before behavioural quality control.
The mean elapsed interval was 11.69 h (SD = 0.48, range 11.13-13.31) in AM-PM and 12.04 h (SD = 0.84, range 11.23-16.97) in PM-AM.
All participants were asked to refrain from daytime sleep during the interval and to avoid excessive caffeine or alcohol.
Adherence was assessed using the delay-interval questionnaire.
After the 12-hour delay, participants received an email link and logged in to complete Session 2.
They first completed the delay-interval questionnaire about activities during the interval and then the Stanford Sleepiness Scale.
Before the delayed test, participants were told for the first time that both direct and indirect association trials would appear.
An example trial illustrated both the 2AFC choice and the subsequent source-memory rating on a 5-point scale.

The delayed test comprised 60 trials, including 40 direct-association trials and 20 novel indirect inference trials testing A-C relationships (see Figure 1 for an illustration of the inference structure).
text.formatted: The delayed test comprised 60 trials, including 40 direct-association trials and 20 novel indirect inference trials testing A-C relationships (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> for an illustration of the inference structure).

text.text: Each trial began with a 500-ms fixation cross, followed by the same 2AFC display as at T1 with a 5,000-ms response window.
For A-C inference trials, A objects served as cues.
After each choice, participants rated whether the association felt direct or indirect on a 5-point scale, with raw responses ranging from1 = "Definitely direct" to5 = "Definitely indirect".
Trials were pseudorandomised to intermix direct and indirect items, and participants were offered brief breaks during the test, including optional 20 s break screens.
The session concluded with a debriefing page.
Preprocessing and quality control Participants who did not complete both sessions were excluded before analysis.
For the remaining complete cases, behavioural quality-control criteria used direct trials (A-B and B-C) only.

Participants were flagged and excluded if any of the following held, with z scores computed across complete cases before behavioural exclusions and using participant-level summaries of direct trials only: (a) direct accuracy at T1 was an extreme low outlier (z < -2.5); (b) direct accuracy at T2 was an extreme low outlier (z < -2.5) with acceptable T1 accuracy (z at T1 ≥ -2.0); (c) the proportion of timeouts at T1 or T2 was an extreme high outlier (z > 2.5), where a timeout was defined as no response within 5,000 ms; or (d) mean T1 choice RT was an extreme low outlier (z < -2.5).
text.formatted: Participants were flagged and excluded if any of the following held, with z scores computed across complete cases before behavioural exclusions and using participant-level summaries of direct trials only: (a) direct accuracy at T1 was an extreme low outlier (z < -2.5); (b) direct accuracy at T2 was an extreme low outlier (z < -2.5) with acceptable T1 accuracy (z at T1 ≥ -2.0); (c) the proportion of timeouts at T1 or T2 was an extreme high outlier (z > 2.5), where a timeout was defined as no response within 5,000 ms; or (d) mean T1 choice RT was an extreme low outlier (z < -2.5).

text.text: Flags were not mutually exclusive.
Trials with no choice within 5,000 ms were coded as incorrect for accuracy analyses and excluded from RT, confidence and source-rating analyses.
Log1p RTs were modelled on all remaining trials, including incorrect responses.
Source ratings were reverse coded so 1 indicated "Definitely indirect" and 5 indicated "Definitely direct", with higher values indicating a stronger sense of direct source.

For descriptive source-classification accuracy, direct-source responses counted as correct for A-B and B-C trials, indirect-source responses counted as correct for A-C trials, and midpoint responses counted as incorrect.
We used Bayesian multilevel models fitted with brms 2.22.0 (Bürkner, 2017), Cmd-StanR 0.9.0 (Gabry et al., 2025), and CmdStan 2.36.0 (Carpenter et al., 2017).
text.formatted: We used Bayesian multilevel models fitted with brms 2.22.0 <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bürkner, 2017)</ref>, Cmd-StanR 0.9.0 <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Gabry et al., 2025)</ref>, and CmdStan 2.36.0 <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Carpenter et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Accuracy outcomes were modelled with Bernoulli likelihoods and logit links, source-rating and confidence outcomes with cumulative-logit ordinal models, and log1p-transformed choice RTs with Gaussian likelihoods.

With the exception of the H3 choice-RT and H4 A-C source-rating models, models were fitted with four chains of 2,000 iterations, including 1,000 warm-up iterations, adapt_delta = 0.95, and max_treedepth = 12.

Because initial diagnostics were comparatively weak for these two models, H3 was refitted with 4,000 iterations, including 2,000 warm-up iterations, and H4 with longer chains and stricter sampler controls.
Sampling diagnostics were evaluated with R-hat, effective sample sizes, and divergent transitions.
Focal hypothesis terms had R-hat values at or below 1.01 and adequate effective sample sizes.
Weakly informative priors were used (intercepts Normal(0, 1.5); coefficients Normal(0, 0.5); standard deviations Student-t(3, 0, 2.5)).
We summarise effects using posterior medians and 95% credible intervals (CrI).
We interpret effects as well-supported when the 95% CrI excludes the null (log-odds 0, odds ratio 1, or .50 for chance tests).

Four further models used the same framework: a refit of the H3 RT model to correct responses only, the H1 and H2 models with centred SSS ratings added, and a model of A-C accuracy for triplets with both premises correct at T1.
These are described in the supplement.
Unless otherwise noted, descriptive summaries are participant-level observed means, whereas model estimates are posterior summaries from the Bayesian multilevel models.
Of the 209 complete cases, 24 participants were flagged and excluded at the initial protocol and behavioural QC stage.

Flags comprised an intersession delay of 18 h or longer (n = 12), low T1 direct accuracy (n = 4), low T2 direct accuracy despite acceptable T1 accuracy (n = 3), high T1 timeout rate (n = 6), high T2 timeout rate (n = 6), and unusually fast T1 RT (n = 0).
Flags were not mutually exclusive, leaving 185 complete cases.
A further 18 AM-PM participants reported sleeping during the daytime delay and were excluded from the primary AM-PM versus PM-AM comparison.
The main analysis sample comprised N = 167, with AM-PM n = 75 and PM-AM n = 92.
Decision timeouts were uncommon.
At T1, 3.5% of direct decisions exceeded the 5,000-ms response window.
At T2, 7.6% of decisions timed out across all trial types.
Among PM-AM participants, mean delay-period sleep duration was 6.4 hours (SD = 2.1), and mean sleep quality was 4.2 (SD = 1.1) on the 6-point scale.
Descriptively, SSS ratings were similar at Session 1 (AM-PM M = 3.07, SD = 1.25; PM-AM M = 3.37, SD = 1.21; one AM-PM participant had no Session 1 rating).

At Session 2, PM-AM participants, tested in the morning, reported greater sleepiness (M = 3.80, SD = 1.48) than AM-PM participants tested in the evening (M = 2.55, SD = 1.30), a difference of 1.26 points.

Because A-C accuracy was low overall, we examined trial-level measures related to A-C decisions.
We asked whether the PM-AM schedule was associated with more indirect source attribution (H4) or weaker dependence on the corresponding premise memories (H5, H6).
At T2, participants rated whether each selected association felt directly learned or indirectly inferred.
Because the ratings were reverse coded for analysis, higher source-rating values indicated stronger direct-source attribution.
Descriptively, source-classification accuracy for direct pairs was 65.3% for A-B and 61.7% for B-C in the AM-PM group.

In the PM-AM group, source-classification accuracy was 67.6% for A-B and 63.9% for B-C. For A-C trials, the proportion correctly classified as indirect was 59.4% in the AM-PM group and 54.7% in the PM-AM group.
The ordinal model provided no clear evidence of a schedule difference in A-C source attribution (OR = 1.07, 95% CrI [0.87, 1.32]).

Because overall A-C accuracy was close to chance, we conducted two exploratory analyses of whether inference was more evident when premise memory was strong, and whether a PM-AM advantage emerged under those conditions.
The first worked at the level of individual triplets, and the second at the level of participants.
Successful A-C inference requires both corresponding premises, so overall A-C accuracy averages over triplets in which one or both premises had been lost.
We therefore estimated A-C accuracy for triplets in which both the A-B and the B-C premise were answered correctly.
For T2 premises, estimates were predictions at two correct premises from the premise-count model.
For T1 premises, they came from a separate model of the qualifying A-C trials (Table 3).

With both premises correct at T2, estimated A-C accuracy was higher than the fullsample estimate in both groups (AM-PM: .61, 95% CrI [.52, .70]; PM-AM: .58, 95% CrI [.48, .67]), and the AM-PM interval excluded chance.
The schedule difference (PM-AM minus AM-PM, in percentage points) was -3.7, 95% CrI [-9.3, 1.8].

Estimates were lower when selection was based on T1 premises (AM-PM: .56, 95% CrI [.45, .66]; PM-AM: .52, 95% CrI [.41, .63]; difference -3.7, 95% CrI [-10.2, 3.4]), consistent with some premises learned at T1 being lost over the delay.
A-C accuracy was therefore highest when both premises were accessible at the delayed test, with no clear evidence of an overnight advantage.
High performers were defined post hoc as participants with delayed direct accuracy of at least .75 averaged across A-B and B-C trials at T2 (n = 97).
In this subgroup, the model-estimated probability of a correct A-C response was .58 [.46, .69], numerically higher than the full-sample estimate, although the 95% CrI included chance.
The AM-PM estimate was .60 [.47, .71], and the PM-AM estimate was .56 [.44, .68].
text.formatted: The AM-PM estimate was .60 [.47, .71], and the PM-AM estimate was .56 <ref type="bibr">[.44, .68</ref>].

text.text: The high-performer analysis therefore gave no clear evidence of an overnight advantage among participants with relatively strong premise memory.
Across outcomes, the PM-AM schedule produced a similar pattern to the AM-PM schedule.
Direct-pair accuracy declined across the intended 12-hour interval in both groups, A-C accuracy remained close to chance, and the A-C response time cost persisted.
In this web-based paired-associate task, explicit inference was similar after overnight and daytime intervals when A-C relations were first tested after the delay.
The response time, source-rating, and premise-memory results were more consistent with retrieval and recombination of the studied pairs than with a newly formed direct A-C shortcut.
A-C responses were slower than direct-pair responses, A-C accuracy was highest on trials judged as clearly indirect, and A-C accuracy increased with premise availability.
These findings suggest that correct A-C responses were constrained by access to the studied A-B and B-C pairs, with the weaker pair acting as a bottleneck when premise memory was fragile.

Although early work reported gains after sleep in hierarchical inference (Ellenbogen et al., 2007; Werchan & Gómez, 2013) and gains after a nap in A-C or relational inference (Alger & Payne, 2016; Lau et al., 2011), later reviews and recent empirical work indicate that such benefits are small and strongly dependent on task demands and outcome measure (Cordi & Rasch, 2021; Lerner & Gluck, 2019).
text.formatted: Although early work reported gains after sleep in hierarchical inference <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Ellenbogen et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Werchan & Gómez, 2013)</ref> and gains after a nap in A-C or relational inference <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Alger & Payne, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Lau et al., 2011)</ref>, later reviews and recent empirical work indicate that such benefits are small and strongly dependent on task demands and outcome measure <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cordi & Rasch, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Lerner & Gluck, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In a closely related visual paired-associate task, Schmidig et al. (2024) reported gains after a nap in recognition discrimination but no reliable benefit for associative cued recall.
text.formatted: In a closely related visual paired-associate task, <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Schmidig et al. (2024)</ref> reported gains after a nap in recognition discrimination but no reliable benefit for associative cued recall.

text.text: Other recent studies report null or modest sleep effects for protection from interference (Bailes et al., 2020; Pöhlchen et al., 2021), selective strengthening of future-relevant memories (Ashton & Cairney, 2021), and abstraction of regularities (Talamini et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Other recent studies report null or modest sleep effects for protection from interference <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bailes et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Pöhlchen et al., 2021)</ref>, selective strengthening of future-relevant memories <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Ashton & Cairney, 2021)</ref>, and abstraction of regularities <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Talamini et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Links between sleep physiology and memory outcomes, such as spindlememory correlations, are also typically small and variable (Kumral et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Links between sleep physiology and memory outcomes, such as spindlememory correlations, are also typically small and variable <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Kumral et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The present results fit this more recent pattern of small or absent sleep benefits.

Accounts of consolidation over sleep, particularly active systems consolidation, propose that recent memories can be stabilised over sleep, sometimes preferentially preserving memories that were stronger or more salient at encoding (Rasch & Born, 2013; Stickgold & Walker, 2013).
text.formatted: Accounts of consolidation over sleep, particularly active systems consolidation, propose that recent memories can be stabilised over sleep, sometimes preferentially preserving memories that were stronger or more salient at encoding <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Rasch & Born, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Stickgold & Walker, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: In the present design, A-B accuracy was generally higher than B-C accuracy, although pair type was tied to both the materials and encoding order.
The design therefore provided an opportunity to detect reduced forgetting overall or preferential preservation of the weaker B-C links.
The Group × Time estimate was centred close to the null, and the A-B/B-C retention gap appeared similar across schedules.
The parallel decline across groups provided no evidence that overnight sleep better preserved directly learned associations under the present remote-testing conditions.

The low A-C accuracy is consistent with retrieval-based accounts in which novel inference at test requires participants to retrieve both A-B and B-C and combine them through the shared B item (Banino et al., 2016; Zeithamova & Preston, 2010).
text.formatted: The low A-C accuracy is consistent with retrieval-based accounts in which novel inference at test requires participants to retrieve both A-B and B-C and combine them through the shared B item <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Banino et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Zeithamova & Preston, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: In the present 2AFC format, identifying the correct A-C relation over a plausible lure depended on retrieving both premises and linking them through the shared B item.
When access to one premise is weak, performance can approach chance even when average premise accuracy is above chance.

This view aligns with the observed increase in A-C success with the number of correctly recognised premises, and it helps explain why any modest preservation of premise memories may not have been sufficient to support novel inference reliably.
The exploratory analyses of strong premise memory further characterised this premise-dependent pattern.
For triplets in which both relevant premises were recognised at T2, A-C accuracy was higher than in the full sample and exceeded chance in the AM-PM group.
Among participants with strong delayed premise memory (≥ .75 accuracy on A-B/B-C at T2), A-C accuracy was numerically higher, although its interval included chance.
Both analyses showed similar performance across schedules, extending the main result beyond the full-sample average.
The encoding schedule may have limited inference.
A-B and B-C pairs were presented in separate blocks (A-B, B-C, A-B, B-C) rather than fully interleaved trial by trial.

Some accounts propose that integration is promoted when encountering an overlapping item (B) triggers retrieval of its earlier associate (A) during encoding of the new associate (C), creating an opportunity for online coactivation and tagging of overlap for later offline processing (Schlichting & Preston, 2015; Shohamy & Wagner, 2008).
text.formatted: Some accounts propose that integration is promoted when encountering an overlapping item (B) triggers retrieval of its earlier associate (A) during encoding of the new associate (C), creating an opportunity for online coactivation and tagging of overlap for later offline processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Schlichting & Preston, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Shohamy & Wagner, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: This blocked structure reduced opportunities for rapid switching between overlapping episodes and may have limited the online coactivation thought to support later integration.
The encoding schedule therefore represents an important boundary condition for interpreting the null sleep effect.
Future work could test this directly by manipulating trial-level interleaving.
Source ratings showed modest differentiation between selected associations on direct and indirect trials.

Because participants were told at T2 that indirect trials would appear, these ratings are best interpreted as subjective judgements about how they made each choice, rather than as direct evidence that an A-C relation had been stored as a new memory.
Source ratings were similar across schedules.
A-C accuracy was highest on trials rated as clearly indirect, whereas accuracy was at or below chance when participants endorsed more direct source ratings.
On successful A-C trials, participants tended to judge the decision as an inference supported by the premises rather than as direct memory for an A-C association.
However, recognising an association as indirect did not guarantee correct responding in a 2AFC task, where both options may be familiar.

This dissociation between structural awareness and item-level discrimination is consistent with source-monitoring and dual-process accounts in which the subjective basis of a response can diverge from the recollective evidence needed to resolve specific alternatives (Johnson et al., 1993; Yonelinas, 2002).
text.formatted: This dissociation between structural awareness and item-level discrimination is consistent with source-monitoring and dual-process accounts in which the subjective basis of a response can diverge from the recollective evidence needed to resolve specific alternatives <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Johnson et al., 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Yonelinas, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: The sleep manipulation was limited by the standard AM-PM versus PM-AM schedule.
Sleep opportunity was confounded with time of day and retrieval state, and the PM-AM group also reported greater sleepiness at Session 2.
Sleep during the delay was assessed by self-report rather than objective monitoring such as actigraphy or polysomnography.

Some AM-PM participants reported interval sleep and were excluded from the primary comparison, which reduced the analysed sample and highlights the difficulty of maintaining a clean daytime-wake contrast in a remote design.
These features limit conclusions about specific sleep physiology.
The task also set a high threshold for detecting small schedule-related effects.
The web-based setting introduced variation in testing environment and response timing, which may have reduced sensitivity to subtle effects on choice RT or inference accuracy.
Presenting A-C trials only at T2 avoided immediate inference testing and reduced test-induced learning, but it also meant that there was no baseline measure of A-C performance before the delay.
Thus, the design assessed delayed explicit inference rather than change in A-C performance across the interval.

The immediate test of the premise pairs may also have reduced the scope for a sleep benefit on direct-pair retention, because sleep can enhance recall of restudied material while leaving recall of previously retrieved material unaffected (Abel et al., 2019; Bäuml et al., 2014).
text.formatted: The immediate test of the premise pairs may also have reduced the scope for a sleep benefit on direct-pair retention, because sleep can enhance recall of restudied material while leaving recall of previously retrieved material unaffected <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abel et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Bäuml et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Low overall A-C accuracy also leaves uncertainty about sensitivity to a small sleep benefit.
This concern does not by itself explain the null effect, because laboratory nap studies have also reported limited sleep benefits for related visual paired-associate outcomes (Schmidig et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This concern does not by itself explain the null effect, because laboratory nap studies have also reported limited sleep benefits for related visual paired-associate outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Schmidig et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Future work should test these boundary conditions with designs that separate schedule effects from sleep more cleanly and that lower uncertainty about the mechanism.

One priority is to manipulate premise strength and encoding structure directly, for example by using criterion learning for A-B and B-C and by comparing trial-level interleaving with separate A-B and B-C blocks.

A second priority is to vary the timing of the inference test by comparing T2-only A-C testing with designs that include an immediate A-C baseline, so that offline change in inference can be separated from delayed inference level.
Interval structure could also be controlled more tightly with nap versus wake designs, counterbalanced schedules, or longer delays that include multiple nights of sleep.
Objective sleep measurement, whether through actigraphy in home settings or polysomnography in the laboratory, would strengthen manipulation validation and allow links to specific sleep features.

Targeted memory reactivation during slow-wave sleep could then test whether externally cued replay is sufficient to improve A-C inference when premise traces are weak to moderate (Hu et al., 2020; Santamaria et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Targeted memory reactivation during slow-wave sleep could then test whether externally cued replay is sufficient to improve A-C inference when premise traces are weak to moderate <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Hu et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Santamaria et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In conclusion, the present findings provide no clear evidence that the overnight PM-AM schedule improved retention of directly learned associations or explicit A-C inference in this paired-associate task.
Instead, A-C success was constrained by the accessibility of the studied premise memories and was strongest when participants experienced their choices as indirect inferences.
These findings suggest that sleeprelated benefits for paired-associate inference, when they occur, may depend on conditions that make premise memories robust and overlapping relations salient.
